newsitem.title: USA: Iowa pork producers await report on PRRS disease.
newsitem.headline: Iowa pork producers await report on PRRS disease.

text.p: Pork producers from the leading pork producing state gathered for their annual meeting here with a sharp eye on an update due Thursday on the seriousness of a hog disease that may have surfaced in Iowa.

"We really don't have a handle on how extensive the problems are with PRRS, or whether a good vaccine will be found here within the next year or so. So it is really tough to define whether it is going to have a great effect or not," said LeRoy Stoltenberg, president of the Iowa Pork Producers Association at the group's Jan 21-23 Pork Congress here.

A U.S. Agriculture Department veterinary team was sent to southeastern Iowa in mid-December to investigate a possible outbreak of a variant of Porcine Reproductive and Respiratory Syndrome (PRRS), an ailment that may have struck several herds. Authorities have kept a tight lid on the probe.
But an update on the veterinarians' findings is likely during the meeting and the pork producers have scheduled a special PRRS news briefing for 0930 CST/1530 GMT Thursday.
The viral disease has caused sows in Iowa to abort fetuses and it also causes lung lesions in all types of swine.
Pork industry sources said other issues generating discussion among producers included environmental rules, the rise of "mega" hog producers, and pork pricing and marketing.
"Keeping current with the latest developments in the industry is absolutely critical for the producer planning to be in operation in the years ahead," Stoltenberg said.

A report this month by the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago pointed to a long-term threat to Iowa and other Midwestern "family farm" pork producers from the rapid rise of "mega" hog farms in states like North Carolina and Missouri.

At end-1995, Iowa's 13.4 million hogs still ranked it number one, but North Carolina's herd shot to 8.2 million from 2.7 million in 1990. In 1995, the average Iowa hog farm had 576 hogs and the average North Carolina farm 1,258 hogs.

Stoltenberg, however, said Iowa's pork industry remained healthy. "Most folks are being cautious because of the price of corn that we had in the past year. But there is still expansion going on in Iowa," he said.
Iowa producers had a banner year in 1996 with cash hog prices reaching a high of $60 per cwt. By midyear, U.S. pork exports were also up 40 percent from a year earlier.
The Congress includes seminars on environmental law and odor control, price forecasting for hogs and grains, and use of the Chicago Mercantile Exchange "lean hog" futures.
